syllabus_version.title: CBSE Curriculum for the Academic Year 2026-27

topics.title: The Havana Riviera disaster and the serpent ring

concepts.learning_objective: Recall the events of the huge wave at the Havana Riviera Hotel and the discovery of the dead woman in the car.
Explain why the gold serpent ring with emerald eyes links the dead woman to the narrator's memory of Frau Frieda.

topics.title: Frau Frieda in Vienna: the woman who sells her dreams

concepts.learning_objective: Identify Frau Frieda's background, her invented name and her claim that she sells her dreams.
Interpret the episode of her brother's death as an illustration of her system of prophecy.
Analyse how her dreams gave her livelihood, authority and wealth in the Viennese family.

topics.title: The meeting in Barcelona with Pablo Neruda

concepts.learning_objective: Describe how the narrator portrays Pablo Neruda's appetite, curiosity and presence.
State how Neruda rejects Frau Frieda's claim to prophetic dreams.
Analyse the mirrored dreams of Neruda and Frau Frieda and the reference to Borges.

topics.title: The ambassador's account, irony and magical realism

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the author and the magical realism that mixes reality with fantasy in the story.
Evaluate the contradiction and the unresolved mystery in the narrator's last exchange with the ambassador.
Analyse the irony in the narrator's attitude to Frau Frieda's dreams.

topics.title: Language work: emphasis, vocabulary and syllables

concepts.learning_objective: Apply the principle that the end of a sentence is its most emphatic position and the middle its least.
Use phrases built on 'dream' and 'sell' with their correct meanings.
Divide words into syllables and count them.

topics.title: James Joyce and the story in context

concepts.learning_objective: Recall the author, the collection and the literary standing of 'Eveline'.
Explain the central concern of the story: an escape within reach that is not seized.

topics.title: Evening at the window: the avenue and home

concepts.learning_objective: Recall Eveline's memories of the field, the neighbours and her family's past.
Interpret what the familiar objects of the room reveal about Eveline's life.
Analyse the symbolism of the window, the dusk and the dusty cretonne.

topics.title: Weighing the decision: home, the Stores and her father

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how Eveline weighs her hard life at home and at the Stores against a new life.
Describe her father's violence and the Saturday quarrels over money.

topics.title: Frank and the promise of Buenos Aires

concepts.learning_objective: Recall who Frank is and how Eveline's feelings for him developed.
Explain why Eveline's father opposed Frank and its effect on the courtship.

topics.title: Memories, the organ and the promise to her mother

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret Eveline's softer memories of her father as her departure nears.
Explain the significance of the street organ, the promise and 'Derevaun Seraun'.

topics.title: At the North Wall: the moment of choice

concepts.learning_objective: Analyse Eveline's paralysis and final response to Frank at the station.
Interpret the emotions evoked by the images in the last section.

topics.title: Language work: parallelism and word stress

concepts.learning_objective: Identify parallel structures and explain how they show similarity or contrast.
Identify the stressed syllable in words taken from the lesson.

topics.title: The author and the burden of the wedding

concepts.learning_objective: Recall key facts about Isaac Bashevis Singer given in the author note.
Explain why Dr Margolin and Gretl regard the Brownsville wedding as a burden.

topics.title: Dr Margolin's past and Gretl
topics.ncert_sections: Section before the first Stop and Think (pp. 23-25)

concepts.learning_objective: Analyse why the outwardly successful Dr Margolin secretly feels a failure.
Describe Gretl's background and how her suffering shapes her conduct.

topics.title: The journey to Brownsville
topics.ncert_sections: Taxi ride and the Eastern Parkway accident (pp. 25-27)

concepts.learning_objective: Identify Dr Margolin's principles and his vanity about his appearance.
Interpret the imagery of the journey and the accident as foreshadowing.

topics.title: The wedding hall and the Senciminers

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the Senciminers' talk keeps returning to the Holocaust dead.
Evaluate the contrast between festive merriment and the memory of death.

topics.title: The encounter with Raizel and the ending
topics.ncert_sections: Raizel episode to the end of the story (pp. 31-35)

concepts.learning_objective: Recall the events of Dr Margolin's meeting with Raizel in the chapel.
Interpret the 'World of Twilight' idea and the ambiguous ending.

topics.title: Language work: sentence variety and word stress

concepts.learning_objective: Classify sentences by structure and explain how variety and tense shape style.
Identify primary and secondary stress in words from the lesson.

topics.title: Joseph Conrad and Captain Hagberd's arrival in Colebrook (the barber's account)

concepts.learning_objective: Recall Conrad's background and explain how the story of Hagberd's past is unfolded through another character's narration.
Explain what brought Captain Hagberd to Colebrook and why the townspeople did not think well of him.
Interpret the barber's sardonic view of Hagberd's craze and his plan to cure it by chaffing.

topics.title: Hagberd's 'tomorrow': his seafaring past and preparations for Harry

concepts.learning_objective: Analyse how Hagberd's hope changes from 'next week' to a permanent 'tomorrow'.
Describe how Hagberd prepares a home and a future for his son's return.
Describe the kind of seaman Hagberd had been and his attitude to the sea.

topics.title: Bessie Carvil, her blind father and her bond with Hagberd

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why Bessie listens to and humours Hagberd's ravings without contradicting him.
Describe the character of old Carvil and his treatment of his daughter.
Compare Hagberd and Carvil as men blinded in different ways.

topics.title: The stranger at the gate: Harry Hagberd returns

concepts.learning_objective: Describe Captain Hagberd's reaction to the stranger who claims to bring news of his son.
Identify Harry's reasons for coming to Colebrook and his first reading of the word 'tomorrow'.
Explain how Bessie becomes convinced that the stranger is really Harry.

topics.title: Harry's restless life and the song of the Gambusinos

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the wandering life Harry has led and why he left home.
Interpret the song of the Gambusinos and its bearing on Harry and Bessie.

topics.title: The climax and ending: Bessie's heartbreak and the everlasting tomorrow

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why Harry's return proves a disappointment for Bessie.
Evaluate the irony of Hagberd's hope surviving the actual return of his son.
Interpret Conrad's remark that every mental state, even madness, has its equilibrium based on self-esteem.

topics.title: Language work: allusion and word stress

concepts.learning_objective: Identify allusions in the story and explain the comparison each makes.
Mark the shift of primary stress when a verb becomes a noun ending in -tion.

topics.title: The author and Tao Ying's bus-ticket habit

concepts.learning_objective: Recall key facts about Bi Shu-min, the author of 'One Centimetre'.
Explain Tao Ying's reasoning about bus tickets and the significance of the story's first sentence.
Evaluate whether the author's portrayal of Tao Ying is sympathetic, critical or realistic.

topics.title: Two tickets on the bus: the ideal mother

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why Tao Ying buys a ticket for Xiao Ye although he is one centimetre short.
Analyse how Tao Ying's wish to be a perfect example shapes her conduct before her son.

topics.title: Lao Chiang's ticket and the temple gate

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the confrontation with the guard over Xiao Ye's height at the temple gate.
Interpret why Tao Ying refuses to buy a second ticket and what the outing costs her son's trust.

topics.title: The flattering scales and the broken trust

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the old woman's 'flattering scales' work and what they suggest about measurement.
Analyse the conflict between Tao Ying and Xiao Ye after the temple incident.

topics.title: The letter, the officials' visit and vindication

concepts.learning_objective: Recall how Tao Ying writes her letter with the advice of 'the Writer'.
Evaluate why Tao Ying refuses compensation and why her final vindication matters to her.

topics.title: Language work: figures of speech and word stress

concepts.learning_objective: Identify similes and metaphors in the story and the elements they compare.
Apply the rule of stress shift in words used both as nouns and verbs.

topics.title: John Milton and the occasion of 'On Shakespeare'

concepts.learning_objective: Recall key facts about John Milton and when he wrote 'On Shakespeare'.
Identify 'On Shakespeare' as an epitaph and explain what makes it unusual.

topics.title: Lines 1-8: no monument of stone is needed

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why the speaker rejects piled stones and a pyramid as a memorial for Shakespeare.
Interpret the idea that Shakespeare has built his own monument in the wonder of his readers.

topics.title: Lines 9-16: Shakespeare's verse and its effect on readers

concepts.learning_objective: Explain the contrast between Shakespeare's 'easy numbers' and 'slow-endeavouring art'.
Interpret how readers, made 'marble' by wonder, become Shakespeare's tomb.

topics.title: Form, diction and poetic devices

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the rhyming couplet form in which the poem is written.
Analyse the poem's use of rhetorical questions and paradox.
Explain archaic forms such as 'star-ypointing' and 'need'st'.

topics.title: Theme: the immortality of art

concepts.learning_objective: Explain the theme that a poet's work outlasts any monument of stone.
Evaluate the speaker's attitude and the diction that builds the tribute.

topics.title: Donne and the metaphysical mode

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the features of metaphysical poetry, such as startling imagery, wit and intellect, as seen in Donne's poem.
Recall the key facts about John Donne given in the introductory note.

topics.title: Morning shadows: love's early secrecy

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the morning shadows stand for the disguises of a young love hidden from others.
Interpret noon, when no shadows fall, as the stage of open and complete love.

topics.title: Afternoon shadows: love's decline

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the afternoon shadows stand for the lovers deceiving each other when love declines.
Analyse the speaker's condition that love must stay at its noon to avoid new shadows.

topics.title: Love as light: the closing couplet and the title

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret the final couplet's image of love as a growing or full constant light.
Evaluate why the poem is called a lecture upon the shadow and to whom it is addressed.

topics.title: Language work: old spellings and adjectives

concepts.learning_objective: Recognise the final 'e' and other old spellings of Donne's period.
Identify how the possessive was written without an apostrophe in Donne's English.
Distinguish the meaning of an adjective in isolation from its meaning in a phrase such as 'infant loves'.

topics.title: John Milton: the poet and his life

concepts.learning_objective: Recall and interpret the key facts of Milton's life, education, blindness and late works given in the introduction.

topics.title: On Time: the race of Time and what it devours

concepts.learning_objective: Explain the images of envious Time, the leaden-stepping hours and the plummet's pace.
Interpret why the loss to humans and the gain to Time are both said to be little.

topics.title: On Time: Eternity and the triumph over Time

concepts.learning_objective: Identify what is associated with the eternal and what guides the soul to the supreme Throne.
Evaluate who finally wins the race against Time and why.

topics.title: On Shakespear: no need of a monument of stone

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why Milton calls a stone monument a 'weak witness' of Shakespeare's name.
Interpret how the readers' wonder becomes Shakespeare's live-long monument.

topics.title: On Shakespear: the reader's tribute and the poet's art

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how Shakespeare's 'easie numbers' and 'Delphic lines' inspire succeeding generations.
Analyse the paradox of readers turned to marble forming a tomb kings would die for.

topics.title: Language Study: etymology

concepts.learning_objective: Define etymology and read the origin note given in a dictionary entry.
Recall the facts about French borrowings into English given in the chapter.

topics.title: William Blake and the Songs of Innocence and of Experience

concepts.learning_objective: Describe Blake as poet, painter and engraver and his view of human beings beset with evil yet striving for the divine.
Explain how Songs of Innocence and Songs of Experience represent the two contrary states of the human soul.
Explain why Blake's method of making each copy of his poems makes him the first multi-media artist.

topics.title: The Divine Image

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how Mercy, Pity, Peace and Love are identified with both God and Man in the poem.
Interpret the images of the human heart, face, form and dress given to the four virtues.
Interpret the poem's claim that the human form divine is to be loved in people of every faith and clime.

topics.title: The Human Abstract: virtues that depend on misery

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why the speaker says Pity and Mercy exist only because of poverty and unhappiness.
Interpret the idea that peace built on mutual fear lasts only till selfish loves increase.
Analyse how Cruelty, with holy fears and tears, plants a false Humility.

topics.title: The Human Abstract: the tree of Mystery in the human brain

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret the images of the dismal shade of Mystery, the fruit of Deceit, the Caterpillar, the Fly and the Raven.
Evaluate the conclusion that the tree of false virtue grows in the human brain and not in Nature.

topics.title: Comparing the poems and language work

concepts.learning_objective: Compare how the two matched poems present the same virtues in the states of innocence and experience.
Explain why abstract words such as Mercy, Cruelty and Mystery are capitalised in the poems.
Identify the syllable pattern and the unstressed-stressed foot in the lines of The Divine Image.

topics.title: The poet and the genesis of the poem

concepts.learning_objective: Recall Coleridge's place among the Romantic poets and his distinctive contribution.
Explain how the poem arose from a dream and why it remained a fragment.

topics.title: Xanadu and the stately pleasure-dome

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the setting of Xanadu, the dome, the gardens and the river Alph.
Distinguish the historical elements of the poem from the imaginary ones.

topics.title: The romantic chasm and the mighty fountain

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret the images of the savage, holy and enchanted chasm.
Analyse the words used to describe the violent movement of water.

topics.title: The sacred river and the ancestral voices

concepts.learning_objective: Trace the course of the sacred river and identify the sound devices that describe it.
Explain the discordant note of the ancestral voices prophesying war.

topics.title: The shadow of the dome: a miracle of rare device

concepts.learning_objective: Analyse the juxtaposition of contrasting images in the sunny dome with caves of ice.
Interpret the images that strike the ear, such as the mingled measure of fountain and caves.

topics.title: The Abyssinian maid and poetic ecstasy

concepts.learning_objective: Recall the vision of the Abyssinian maid and the meaning of dulcimer.
Evaluate how the poet likens poetic ecstasy to a divine, magical frenzy.

topics.title: Emily Dickinson: the poet and her style

concepts.learning_objective: Recall the key facts about Emily Dickinson's secluded life and her largely posthumous publication.
Identify the features of Dickinson's style, such as unconventional capitalisation and dashes, and explain their effect.

topics.title: The swaying trees and the music of summer

concepts.learning_objective: Explain the simile of the trees swinging like tassels and the tune rising from tiny creatures.
Interpret 'Far Psalteries of Summer' as the faint, unsatisfying yet enchanting music of summer.

topics.title: The capricious Sun

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the Sun is personified as a whimsical owner of 'Estates of Cloud'.
Explain why the pronouns referring to the Sun are capitalised.

topics.title: Creatures and flowers of the summer day

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the lines in which the bird and other creatures are given human qualities.
Interpret the image of flowers opening from the calyx like 'Hindered Flags'.

topics.title: Nature beyond the painter's art

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why the poet feels even Vandyke's painting falls short of the real summer day.
Show how the poem grows out of close observation of natural phenomena.
Recognise the psaltery and the dulcimer as similar stringed musical instruments.

topics.title: The poet and the autumn setting

concepts.learning_objective: Recall the key facts about W.B. Yeats given with the poem: Irish poet, dramatist and mystic, Irish Literary Revival, Abbey Theatre and the 1923 Nobel Prize.
Interpret the autumn images of the first stanza and connect them to the poet's own stage of life.

topics.title: The count and the swans' sudden flight

concepts.learning_objective: Explain the significance of the nineteenth autumn since the poet first counted the swans.
Describe how the swans rise and scatter in 'great broken rings' and what the image conveys.

topics.title: The poet's changed heart

concepts.learning_objective: Explain what 'the lighter tread' and 'my heart is sore' refer to in the poet's life.
Analyse how the line 'All's changed' expresses the effect of time on the speaker.

topics.title: The unchanging swans and human life

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the qualities of the swans described in the fourth stanza: unwearied, paired, and with hearts that have not grown old.
Compare the timeless vitality of the swans with ageing and changing human life.

topics.title: Mystery, beauty and the fear of loss

concepts.learning_objective: Explain what contributes to the beauty and mystery of the swans' lives in the last stanza.
Interpret the closing question about waking to find the swans have flown away.

topics.title: Language study: rhyme scheme and poetic devices

concepts.learning_objective: Work out the rhyme scheme of a stanza by giving a new letter to every new end sound.
Identify poetic devices in the poem such as compound words, personification and contrast.

topics.title: The poet and the poem's opening

concepts.learning_objective: Recall A.K. Ramanujan's work as poet, translator and scholar and relate it to the poem.
Interpret the effect of the poem's opening with 'Or listen to the clocktowers'.

topics.title: The clocktowers and their discordant time

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the accidental reasons the poem gives for the clocks keeping different times.
Interpret the sound imagery of the gongs and the irony of the 'well-managed city'.

topics.title: Clocks and communities

concepts.learning_objective: Explain the implicit comparison between the clocks and the city's religious communities.
Analyse what cuts off the sound of the gongs and what this suggests about city life.

topics.title: The silenced clock and the title

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret the image of the eyeless, silent clock after its destruction.
Analyse how the poem sets human violence beside a 'precise act of nature'.
Evaluate the double meaning of the title 'Time and Time Again'.

topics.title: The crumbling ancestral house
topics.ncert_sections: Stanzas 1-2 ('When we were children' to 'To watch it die')

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the images of physical and ritual decay through which the great-grandmother describes the three-hundred-year-old house.
Explain why the decline of the house causes the great-grandmother deep personal grief.

topics.title: The childhood promise and the great-grandmother's past
topics.ncert_sections: Stanzas 3-4 ('When I grow old, I said' to 'died of fever, in her arms')

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret the child's promise to rebuild the house and the great-grandmother's response to it.
Describe the great-grandmother's deep faith and her memories of a wealthy, royal past.

topics.title: The 'oldest blood' and class distinction
topics.ncert_sections: Stanza 5 ('She told us / That we had the oldest blood' to 'muddy as a ditch')

concepts.learning_objective: Explain the great-grandmother's pride in the family's 'oldest blood' and the values it reflects.
Analyse how the poem presents and questions the class prejudice behind the idea of superior blood.

topics.title: The death of the great-grandmother and the house
topics.ncert_sections: Stanzas 6-8 ('Finally she lay dying' to 'the dark rooms heave a sigh')

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret what the grown-up poet has learnt about the difficulty of growing rich and keeping her promise.
Analyse how the great-grandmother's death is linked with the dying house through personification.

topics.title: Leaving home: guilt and the conflict of conscience
topics.ncert_sections: Stanzas 9-11 ('I set forth again' to 'Elephant ride...')

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the decay of the abandoned house as the poet imagines it from distant towns.
Evaluate the poet's guilt, her plea for forgiveness and the conflict in her conscience.

topics.title: The poet, poetic devices and style
topics.ncert_sections: Introduction to the poet; Language Study

concepts.learning_objective: Recall key facts about Kamala Das and her place in Indian writing.
Identify and interpret the similes, personification and other images used in the poem.
Compare the free verse and conversational idiom of 'Blood' with earlier English poetry such as Donne's.

topics.title: Non-fiction and Shaw's idea of a perfectly free person

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the forms and purpose of non-fiction writing as described in the section introduction.
Explain why Shaw holds that no person can be perfectly free because of natural necessities.

topics.title: Natural slavery and the slavery of man to man
topics.ncert_sections: Freedom (G.B. Shaw), on stolen labour, governments and Nature

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how, according to Shaw, one class shifts its share of labour on to another.
Interpret Shaw's criticism of governments, elections and the vote.
Distinguish the pleasant slavery to Nature from the hateful slavery of man to man.

topics.title: The humbug of freedom and the delusion of the master class
topics.ncert_sections: Freedom (G.B. Shaw), on propaganda, the gentleman and human nature

concepts.learning_objective: Recall the historical events that people are taught to see as victories for freedom.
Explain why Shaw thinks the master class is more deluded than the enslaved masses.
Evaluate the two views Shaw presents on whether human nature can be changed.

topics.title: Restrictions on freedom and freedom as leisure

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the ways in which laws, landlords and employers restrict individual freedom.
Explain Shaw's view of the strike and the general strike.
Interpret Shaw's advice to call freedom leisure and to work out how much of it a worker has.

topics.title: Understanding Freedom and Discipline (J. Krishnamurti)

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why Krishnamurti considers discipline and freedom contradictory.
Analyse how conformity to tradition prevents the growth of intelligence.
Explain how fear and self-concern destroy sensitivity.

topics.title: Language work: sentence types, rhetorical questions and sound sequences

concepts.learning_objective: Classify sentences as simple, complex or compound and identify main clauses.
Infer the implied statement behind a rhetorical question.
Write the consonant-vowel sound sequence of a word.
